Vs.

full_judgment:
The appellant, Nur Banu, took pattan of the suit lands from Nurun Nahar Bibi, predecessor-in-interest of the respondents, by executing a registered kabuliyat, Ext. 1 on February 21, 1950 and since then she had been living there by constructing huts thereon. By a notice sent by registered post on 13.10.59 and also the notice through court on 11.10.59 the appellant was directed to vacate the suit land by the end of the Bangalee calendar year. 

 6. According to the learned Counsel if the lease is from year to year which, in his opinion it is, the notice to vacate should have been given six months prior to the end of the year of the lease, and not with the end of the calendar year. A.s the kabuliyat was registered on 9th Falgoon, 1356 B.S, corresponding to February 21, 1950 the period under notice should have ended on 8th Falgoon of the year in which notice was given Instead of this, the notice which was served by registered post on 25th Aswin. 1366 B.S. asked the appellant to vacate by 30th Chaitra, 1366 B.S. As no particular date has been mentioned in the kabuliyat as to when the lease commenced, according to Mr. Khondker it commenced" from the date of making of the lease. In this connection the learned Counsel referred to the provisions of section 110 of the Transfer of Property Act which provides as follows:- 

 8. In answering the incidental question which cropped up during the course of arguments as to whether the applicant can at all raise any objection as to the sufficiency of the period of notice, Mr. Khonker emphatically asserted that the plaintiff-respondent must succeed on the strength of her own case. For, he mentioned though the defendant-appellant did not rely on the kabuliyat, it is the plaintiff-respondent's cast that the kabuliyat in question was executed by the defendant-appellant. Mention may be made that in her written statement it was alleged that the kabuliyat was obtained by fraud and was not, therefore, a valid document. In support of the principle that the plaintiff must succeed on the strength of his own case, Mr. Khondker cited the case of Jagadish Narian Vs. Nawab Said Ahmed Khan, (1945) 50 CWN PC 477. The principle, though elementary is no doubt important but when the very foundation of the plaintiff-respondent's claim has totally been denied by the defendant-appellant who dismissed the kabuliyat as a fraudulent transaction, it is difficult to concede that the defendant-appellant should be allowed to rely on a point whose validity depends upon the acceptance of the document itself, which can give rise to such point. Expediency is not an unknown phenomenon in the legal arena, but the principles of approbation and reapprobation are also equally well known. A party to a Suit after taking an exact stand in his plain or written" statement cannot so readily be allowed to depart from it on the ground that his opponent admitted the position which was opposite to his stand, Justice and expediency cannot go together. 

 10. In her written statement the defendant-appellant discarded the registered kabuliyat, Ext. 1 as having been obtained by the predecessor of the plaintiff-respondent fraudulently. After having done so, she cannot now be allowed to raise objections as to the requirement of sufficiency of six months' notice relying on the kabuliyat itself upon which the plaintiff-respondent tried to build up her case. Moreover, it does not appear that the defendant-appellant raised this point before. In none of the courts below, this point regarding the sufficiency of notice was raised. In the absence of such objection at the relevant stage, facts necessary to determine the sufficiency or otherwise of the notice served upon the defendant-appellant could not be determined. As pointed out by Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, Counsel for the plaintiff respondent, that if at the trial stage or even after remand by the High Court Division, the defendant-appellant raised objection. on this score, it would have been open to the plaintiff-respondent to bring evidence on this point, but after the lapse of 24 years since notice had been served upon the defend ant-appellant this objection, if accepted, would put them to a great disadvantage. Any such objection if raised at the earlier stage would have enabled the plaintiff-respondent to adduce evidence on this point or even to withdraw the suit and after serving a fresh notice could have filed another suit. It may be mentioned that the trial court dismissed the suit on the finding that no notice under section 9(1) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act was served upon the defendant-appellant. On appeal the case was sent back on remand against which the plaintiff-respondent filed a Second Miscellaneous Appeal. After setting aside the order of remand the High Court Division directed the first appellate court to decide the appeal on merit and to take additional evidence if necessary, to prove the service of notice. Before that court the only point raised as to whether the suit was maintainable or not was decided in favour of the plaintiff-respondent and against the defendant-appellant who, being aggrieved moved the High Court Division which Court also held that there was service of notice upon the defendant-appellant. I do not think that in the circumstances as stated above, the defendant-appellant has any right to ask for such concession from the court. From the date of registration of the kabuliyat, Mr. Khondker wants to show, the lease started and counting therefrom the lease, being for a year, ended on 8th Falgoon of the next year. Notice terminating the tenancy should, therefore, have preceded six months prior to this date and the period of six months under notice should have ended precisely on 8th Falgoon of the year of notice. As notice given by the predecessor of the plaintiff- respondent did not expire on 8th Falgoon, 1366 B.S. but ended on 30th Chaitra of the same year, the period under notice, though more than six months, such notice did not suffice. It was not a valid notice under law to show when the notice terminating a tenancy as required under law becomes valid, Mr. Khondker cited a few cases. 

 11. In Kishori Mohun Roy Chowdhury vs. Nund Kumar Ghosal, (1897) ILR 24 Cal. 720 it was held that the notice to quit must be served upon the tenant six months prior to the end of the year of the tenancy. Here, the tenancy was created by a kabuliyat with an annual rent reserved. 

 14. Reference may be made to the contention of Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, Counsel for the plaintiff-respondent that the kabuliyat in question, being a document executed unilaterally by one of the parties only, it could not be termed as a lease to which the provisions of section 106 or 110 would apply, because it is provided in section 107 that "where a lease of immovable property is made by a registered instrument, such instrument or where there are more instruments than one, each such instrument shall be executed by both the lessor and the lessee". The point, it would appear, is well taken.
